title: Heterogeneous diffusion with recruitment and mortality
authors: Esther D. Gutiérrez, Alexander López, R. K. Singh, Sébastien Fumeron, Malte Henkel, Trifce Sandev
abstract: We study a heterogeneous diffusion process with a position-dependent diffusion coefficient in the presence of independent recruitment and mortality. This framework generalises heterogeneous diffusion under stochastic resetting, which is recovered as the special case of equal recruitment and mortality rates. At long times, the system approaches a non-equilibrium stationary state with a mean squared displacement that saturates to a value independent of the recruitment rate. Crucially, this saturation limit directly encodes the underlying transport regime via an effective exponent applied to the diffusion coefficient, and we characterise the non-trivial transition to this stationary regime. We further derive the mean first-passage time to a target and show that, for a fixed recruitment-to-mortality ratio, an optimal mortality rate minimises the search time. This "mortality-assisted search" effect is confirmed by numerical evaluation. Reinterpreting recruitment and mortality as infection and removal processes, we apply the model to epidemic spreading and show that a moderate removal rate can counter-intuitively accelerate, rather than delay, the arrival of infection at a new spatial region. Beyond epidemiology, our framework offers broad relevance to systems featuring concurrent particle creation and destruction, such as bacterial growth, tracer diffusion in reactive fluids, or cellular population dynamics in crowded environments.
summary: This work models diffusion in an open environment subject to particle creation (recruitment) and decay (mortality). It establishes that the system reaches a stable, non-equilibrium state characterized by a saturated Mean Squared Displacement. Crucially, it reveals a 'mortality-assisted search' effect, showing that intermediate decay rates can optimize the speed of reaching a target region.
main_problem: The paper investigates heterogeneous diffusion in open systems characterized by continuous particle creation (recruitment) and destruction (mortality). It analyzes how these processes affect transport properties and search times.
main_result: The system reaches a non-equilibrium stationary state where the Mean Squared Displacement saturates to a value independent of the recruitment rate. Furthermore, a moderate mortality rate can counter-intuitively accelerate the arrival of an infection at a new spatial region.
method: The analysis involves deriving the probability density function and survival probabilities using modified Fokker-Planck equations and the dynamic redundancy framework. Long-time asymptotic behavior is analyzed using Laplace approximations.
model_or_system: The model is a Heterogeneous Diffusion Process (HDP) with a position-dependent diffusion coefficient $D(x) \propto |x|^\alpha$. The process is open, incorporating independent recruitment ($\lambda$) and mortality ($\mu$) rates.
key_observables: Mean Squared Displacement ($\langle x^2(t) angle$), survival probability $S(t)$, and mean first-passage time $\langle T angle$.
important_parameters: Heterogeneity exponent ($\alpha$), recruitment rate ($\lambda$), and mortality rate ($\mu$).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes a specific power-law form for the diffusion coefficient $D(x)$ and relies on approximations like the Laplace method for long-time limits.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the saturation of survival probabilities ($S(t)$) and the non-monotonic dependence of the mean first-passage time ($\langle T angle$) on the mortality rate ($\mu$), showing an optimal rate exists.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from deriving the governing equations for the open HDP, calculating the long-time saturation of the MSD, analyzing the first-passage time using survival probabilities, and finally applying the framework to physical examples like epidemiology.
why_interesting: The framework of open systems with particle creation/destruction and anomalous diffusion is highly relevant to modeling non-equilibrium dynamics in complex physical systems, which shares mathematical structures with open quantum systems.
